front: A signal \(x(t) = 4\cos(2\pi \cdot 1500 t) + 2\cos(2\pi \cdot 4000 t)\) is to be sampled and perfectly reconstructed. What is the minimum sampling rate?
explanation: 1) Identify the frequency components: \(f_1 = 1500\ \text{Hz}\) and \(f_2 = 4000\ \text{Hz}\). 2) The highest frequency present is \(f_{\max} = 4000\ \text{Hz}\). 3) The Nyquist rate is \(f_s = 2 f_{\max} = 2(4000) = 8000\ \text{Hz}\).

front: A \(700\ \text{Hz}\) sinusoid is sampled at \(f_s = 1000\ \text{Hz}\). What apparent frequency appears in the baseband \([0,\ f_s/2]\)?
explanation: 1) The folding (Nyquist) frequency is \(f_s/2 = 500\ \text{Hz}\). 2) Since \(700\ \text{Hz} > 500\ \text{Hz}\), the tone aliases. 3) The alias falls at \(|f - f_s| = |700 - 1000| = 300\ \text{Hz}\), which lies in \([0,\ 500]\ \text{Hz}\).

front: A signal is band-limited to \(20\ \text{kHz}\) and sampled at exactly the Nyquist rate. What is the maximum allowable time between samples?
explanation: 1) The Nyquist rate is \(f_s = 2 f_{\max} = 2(20\ \text{kHz}) = 40\ \text{kHz}\). 2) The sampling interval is \(T_s = 1/f_s = 1/40000\). 3) \(T_s = 25\times 10^{-6}\ \text{s} = 25\ \mu\text{s}\).

front: A \(1200\ \text{Hz}\) tone is sampled at \(f_s = 1000\ \text{Hz}\) and then passed through an ideal low-pass reconstruction filter. At what frequency does the recovered tone appear?
explanation: 1) The Nyquist frequency is \(f_s/2 = 500\ \text{Hz}\); since \(1200 > 500\), aliasing occurs. 2) Subtract the sampling frequency: \(1200 - 1000 = 200\ \text{Hz}\). 3) \(200\ \text{Hz}\) lies within \([0,\ 500]\ \text{Hz}\), so the tone is reconstructed at \(200\ \text{Hz}\).

front: Find the fundamental period of \(x(t) = \cos(2\pi \cdot 50 t) + \cos(2\pi \cdot 75 t)\).
explanation: 1) The component frequencies are \(50\ \text{Hz}\) and \(75\ \text{Hz}\). 2) The fundamental frequency is their greatest common divisor: \(f_0 = \gcd(50, 75) = 25\ \text{Hz}\). 3) The period is \(T_0 = 1/f_0 = 1/25 = 0.04\ \text{s} = 40\ \text{ms}\) (check: \(50 = 2 f_0\), \(75 = 3 f_0\)).

front: A signal sampled at \(f_s = 8\ \text{kHz}\) is analyzed with a \(1024\)-point DFT. What is the frequency spacing between adjacent DFT bins?
explanation: 1) The DFT bin spacing is \(\Delta f = f_s / N\). 2) Substitute \(f_s = 8000\ \text{Hz}\) and \(N = 1024\). 3) \(\Delta f = 8000/1024 = 7.8125\ \text{Hz}\).

front: A periodic signal has fundamental period \(T = 5\ \text{ms}\). What is the frequency of the third harmonic in its Fourier series?
explanation: 1) The fundamental frequency is \(f_0 = 1/T = 1/0.005 = 200\ \text{Hz}\). 2) The \(n\)th harmonic is located at \(n f_0\). 3) The third harmonic is \(3 f_0 = 3(200) = 600\ \text{Hz}\).

front: Compute the convolution \(y[n] = x[n] * h[n]\) of \(x[n] = \{1, 2, 3\}\) (for \(n = 0,1,2\)) and \(h[n] = \{1, 1\}\) (for \(n = 0,1\)).
explanation: 1) The output length is \(3 + 2 - 1 = 4\). 2) Compute term by term: \(y[0] = 1\cdot 1 = 1\); \(y[1] = 1\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 1 = 3\); \(y[2] = 2\cdot 1 + 3\cdot 1 = 5\); \(y[3] = 3\cdot 1 = 3\). 3) Thus \(y[n] = \{1, 3, 5, 3\}\).

front: A length-\(20\) sequence is convolved (linear convolution) with a length-\(8\) sequence. What is the length of the resulting sequence?
explanation: 1) For linear convolution of sequences of lengths \(N\) and \(M\), the output length is \(N + M - 1\). 2) Substitute \(N = 20\) and \(M = 8\). 3) Length \(= 20 + 8 - 1 = 27\).

front: A discrete-time signal \(x[n]\) is convolved with the shifted unit impulse \(\delta[n-2]\). What is \(x[n] * \delta[n-2]\)?
explanation: 1) Convolution with a unit impulse reproduces the signal: \(x[n] * \delta[n] = x[n]\). 2) Convolving with a shifted impulse shifts the signal by that amount (sifting property). 3) Therefore \(x[n] * \delta[n-2] = x[n-2]\).

1) Start from the standard pair \((0.5)^n u[n] \leftrightarrow \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.5 z^{-1}}\). 2) The given signal is that sequence delayed by 2 samples: \(x[n] = g[n-2]\) with \(g[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]\). 3) The time-shift property \(g[n-k] \leftrightarrow z^{-k} G(z)\) gives \(X(z) = \dfrac{z^{-2}}{1 - 0.5 z^{-1}}\).

front: A causal discrete-time system has transfer function \(H(z) = \dfrac{z}{z - 0.9}\). Give the pole location and state whether the system is stable.
explanation: 1) Poles occur where the denominator is zero: \(z - 0.9 = 0 \Rightarrow z = 0.9\). 2) A causal LTI system is BIBO stable when all poles lie inside the unit circle. 3) Since \(|0.9| < 1\), the pole is inside the unit circle, so the system is stable.

front: A causal LTI system obeys the difference equation \(y[n] = x[n] + 0.5\,y[n-1]\). Find its transfer function \(H(z)\) and impulse response \(h[n]\).
explanation: 1) Take the \(z\)-transform of both sides: \(Y(z) = X(z) + 0.5 z^{-1} Y(z)\). 2) Collect \(Y(z)\): \(Y(z)(1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) = X(z)\), so \(H(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 - 0.5 z^{-1}}\). 3) Inverting the standard pair gives \(h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]\).

front: A 4-point moving-average filter is \(y[n] = \tfrac{1}{4}\big(x[n] + x[n-1] + x[n-2] + x[n-3]\big)\). What is its DC (zero-frequency) gain?
explanation: 1) The DC gain equals the sum of the impulse-response coefficients, i.e. \(H(z)\) evaluated at \(z = 1\). 2) Each coefficient is \(1/4\), so the sum is \(4 \times \tfrac{1}{4} = 1\). 3) A gain of \(1\) is \(20\log_{10}(1) = 0\ \text{dB}\).

front: An FIR filter has an impulse response with \(11\) taps (coefficients \(h[0]\) through \(h[10]\)). What is the order of the filter?
explanation: 1) The order of an FIR filter is the highest power of \(z^{-1}\) in \(H(z)\). 2) With taps \(h[0], \dots, h[10]\), the highest-delay term is \(z^{-10}\). 3) Therefore the order is \(N - 1 = 11 - 1 = 10\).

front: A discrete-time filter has transfer function \(H(z) = \dfrac{1 + z^{-1}}{2}\). Is it a low-pass or a high-pass filter?
explanation: 1) Evaluate the gain at DC (\(z = 1\), i.e. \(\omega = 0\)): \(H = \tfrac{1 + 1}{2} = 1\). 2) Evaluate at the highest frequency (\(z = -1\), i.e. \(\omega = \pi\)): \(H = \tfrac{1 - 1}{2} = 0\). 3) It passes DC and rejects the highest frequency, so it is a low-pass filter.
